Bobby Fischer® Learn to Play Chess Set Board Game, Easy to Understand - How to Play Chess Book, 34 Plastic Staunton Chess Pieces, Folding Illustrated Chess Board, Family Games for Kids and Adults When I was in middle school, a teacher I did not really know invited me in to learn chess. It changed my life. I wanted to pass the information on to my kids, but it was hard to get them to make connections. This set is great.

WHAT IS THIS SET LIKE?
This set comes with a four fold board, big sized pieces, general instructions, and two dice.

BOARD
The board has information right on it, so that you don't have to repeat it over and over for visual learners.

PIECES
The pieces in this box are plenty big enough, have a nice felt bottom and are all in the box. Nothing was missing. There were even the two extra queens in the box too.

IS IT EASY TO TEACH WITH?
I found that this is really easy to teach with and in my case, it has been a while since I could play chess with someone and not a computer, so I found this very exciting.

DICE
The dice is a great way to even out playing with a beginner which helps a lot because who wants to be beaten constantly?

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a great set for a beginner chess learner. The board is small, the pieces easy to use and the directions clear and well laid out. The dice make it fun for mis matched players (beginner vs more advanced).

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I like this set and am glad to have it. My family is finally going to learn chess without me having to continually explain everything. The visuals are great.
text_fidelity_b: Bobby Fischer® Learn to Play Chess Set Board Game, Easy to Understand - How to Play Chess Book, 34 Plastic Staunton Chess Pieces, Folding Illustrated Chess Board, Family Games for Kids and Adults

Buffalo Games - Vintage America - 2000 Piece Jigsaw Puzzle [[VIDEOID:70993f24c2cce65d6b7aea10ebd6a5fc]] This is an awesome puzzle! It was so much fun to put together. It's actually pretty easy for a 2000 piece puzzle, because of all of the different colors and patterns. I'm not saying it's super easy, because any 2000 piece puzzle is an intense challenge. But, it has lots of clear detail, and with most of the pieces, you're able to get a pretty good idea of where it actually goes by looking at the picture. That makes a puzzle fun and not frustrating. The hardest part to do was actually the "America" part, because it had a lot of solid red. But overall, all of the parts of the puzzle went at a pretty good pace.

They include a poster print out with an enlarged full picture of the puzzle, which I really like, especially because the box picture has some of the picture obscured. They fully exclude Hawaii and Alaska, so you might get a little upset if you're from either of those fine states. But, aesthetically I think it was a good choice.

The pieces are medium sized and above medium quality. It's a good solid puzzle, probably about Ravensburger quality, which is mid-range for puzzles.

text_fidelity_a:
Imagine Meditation Kit for Kids - Award-Winning Mindfulness kit of XL Cards with Calming Guided Meditations for Empowerment, Focus and Relaxation. Great for Parents, Teachers and Therapists. This kit was made to help families like ours. I am a stay at home mom to four kids (11yo and younger). Prior, I was an artist and earned a Special Ed and a Rehabilitation degree. My background has been useful because we ended up a household full of ADHD, severe anxiety, learning and speech disabilities, plus more. We have been using this set for three weeks now and it has proven invaluable. It truly was an excellent find.

We do not own the original set (with the Dove on the box), but I suspect this new version is probably an upgraded improvement of the first box set. It looks very similar, except now there appears have some new (maybe better) ideas and slightly more guidance in this new version. I don't mean to imply this set is a duplicate of the first set, nor am I trying to discourage you from buying both. I simply don't know. I came to the conclusion that these were similar after reading the reviews for the first one. Had I been given the option to chose between the two sets, I would have chosen to start with the newer set I am reviewing here today. Simply because of the changes that were made.

ABOUT THE PRODUCT:

- Most of the cards appear to have between 200 to 300 words. Each activity lasts about 5 minutes per card, give or take. Of course each could be longer or shorter because you get decide how much time you want to spend.

- This newer set has a total of 24 meditation activity cards. 18 of the 24 are guided scenarios. The 18 cards are "story like, short guided imaginary meditation with different scenes that people can imagine themselves taking a part of.” Meaning they ask you to concentrate and imagine yourself in a particular story line (like "walking through the woods" or "stargazing on a warm summer night", for example).
- 6 of those 18 cards mentioned above focus on our senses (touch, taste, etc).
- In addition to the above 18, there are 6 more "positive affirmation" cards. These affirmations address different times of day (morning or bedtime) -or- feelings (anger, stress, etc).

OTHER COMPARISON NOTES:
- From what I can tell, the original set only appears to have 23 guided imaginary "walk through the woods" type scenarios. It does not specifically explore common human experiences that center around feeling or our body.
- The Legend Card is unique to this set. The Legend is more of a guide chart that will help you quickly find the most useful card, depending on the your feelings/needs at the moment­.
- Both sets have the same breathing exercise card.

MY POSITIVES:

- This set is excellent quality. The cards are very nice and are made of a thick paperboard. They are technically laminated, though it wouldn't consider it a plastic waterproof type of covering. It feels more like a wax coating that is water resistant. But it is a sturdy material.
-This truly is an activity for all ages. Kids 6 and younger will probably need guidance. Around 6 or 7, this could probably be an independent activity for most kids. But this mediation set is NOT just for kids. I think pre-teens, teens, and even adults can still benefit from these cards. I wish I made more time to use them myself, tbh.
- These have been excellent in helping everyone in our house decompress and cope with our daily stressors.
- I think this encourages and even teaches how to use our imaginations better (an essential skill!!!).
- It has increases our awareness of self worth. And in a sense, these also teach us to take responsibility for some of our thoughts and feelings too. These activities seem to encourage future motivation and action too.
-This kit is secular and inclusive. Meaning it is not religions in any way. And Many people are represented in the images. The language the cards use, and the activities are age and gender neutral. The suggested scenarios are something anyone can envision.
- And the art is beautiful.

THE NEGATIVES:
- The box is terrible. It's too small. It's impossible to find the one card the Ledged Guide tells you to grab without taking out the entire stack. And it's a pain putting the cards away. I'm going to have to come up with a better storage system.
- There are spelling mistakes, improper punctuation, and unnecessary capitalization. If it had been here or there, I wouldn't have said anything. Nor am I in a position to judge. But it's really bad and does not feel educational.
- The price feels a bit steep initially. However, I think if you make it a goal to give this set a real try and use it for a little while, I think you'll see the $30 price tag actually feels like a good deal.

Overall, I definitely recommend trying this. It is unique and I wish I had know about the original set years ago. But I think this newer set was an even better find. We couldn't be happier. Thank you for reading this ridiculously long review and I hope it helped make your decision easier.
text_fidelity_b: Imagine Meditation Kit for Kids - Award-Winning Mindfulness kit of XL Cards with Calming Guided Meditations for Empowerment, Focus and Relaxation. Great for Parents, Teachers and Therapists.

text_fidelity_a:
Ravensburger Neuschwanstein Castle 2000 Piece Panorama XXL Jigsaw Puzzle for Adults – Softclick Technology Means Pieces Fit Together Perfectly This NEUSCHWANSTEIN CASTLE XXL puzzle is not for beginners, or for the faint of heart! Any 2000-piece Ravensburger puzzle is difficult, simply because of the number of pieces, but this puzzle is probably above average in difficulty.

The puzzle measures 52" wide by 24" high--it's a panoramic puzzle--so make sure you have cleared a wide space for it. The XXL size means that the fine photo details are spread over more than one puzzle piece, and this increases the difficulty. The puzzle is easiest to assemble if you stand over it as you go, so that you can see the bigger, overall picture.

Ravensburger puzzles always have color areas to help you. That's true of this puzzle, but the sky--there's lots of it!-- has less color variation than usual. The border pieces are easy to find and assemble, but when you start on the remaining puzzle, it really dawns on you what a challenging task you have undertaken. There are piles of dark blue, light blue, autumn-colored, and mostly-white pieces that look very much alike. For me, the hardest area was the lower left side, with all of the blue trees; and the big snow-covered tree at the right was far more difficult than I expected. The castle was easy, and the autumn-colored trees were easier than you would think from looking at the box photo.

Despite its difficulty, this puzzle was a pleasure to work. The photo is just so beautiful! Working at a comfortable pace (one to several hours at a stretch, but not every day), I needed about a month to finish this one. As usual, I found the Ravensburger craftsmanship to be extraordinary--the pieces fit together so nicely that mistakes were few and far between. I highly recommend this puzzle for expert (addicted) jigsaw puzzle enthusiasts.
text_fidelity_b: Ravensburger Neuschwanstein Castle 2000 Piece Panorama XXL Jigsaw Puzzle for Adults – Softclick Technology Means Pieces Fit Together Perfectly

SUPER MARIO Boo's Mansion Kids Halloween Hide-and-Seek Game with 10 Figurines and Accessories We had so much fun with this. While we did not do the whole party element with people watching us unbox, we had a great time just on a normal day when the kids had done a great job, having a special treat of opening up each of the flaps to see what was inside.

A glow-in-the-dark boo, another boo, both with movable arms, a skeleton for around the plant and a dry bones were the highlights for us in this set. The Princess peach, also was detailed to an extent I have never seen on any of our other Princess peach figures. Usually they just fill in and under her skirt with solid plastic, and this one they gave her legs, undershorts, and high-heeled shoes underneath her dress so it is much more of a realistic figure than usual. I think either Mario or Luigi, needed a little plastic stand to be able to stand up and not just topple over. I would've appreciated a little more design on those guys so that they could be played with without an additional little clear plastic stand.

The flap opening and unveiling of the characters was a lot of fun. The characters were almost impossible in some cases to get out of the container without completely destroying the entire packaging, so my kids had to be flexible to wait until we were done opening all the flaps, then tear open the packaging to be able to push from the back and get some of those characters out. However, they were definitely firmly and securely packaged in there and were not going anywhere or getting damaged with those vacuum formed spots to sit.

Overall this was a lot of fun, and with the excellent quality of the figures, made for a very special and memorable gifting event to the kids.
text_fidelity_b: SUPER MARIO Boo's Mansion Kids Halloween Hide-and-Seek Game with 10 Figurines and Accessories

Kinetic Sand, Bake Shoppe Playset with 1lb of Kinetic Sand and 16 Tools and Molds, for Ages 3 and up I have mixed feelings about this set because my kids absolutely loved playing with the kinetic sand. Loved it. The bakeshop playset idea was fun, and while the small number of creative tools made it so that my children were asking for their Play-Doh tools to go with it almost immediately, the new texture was so much fun for them that I cannot give this a poor review. I also loved that we had a miniature Barbie Chelsea sandbox with some sandbox toys, and this kinetic sand filled the sandbox perfectly and allowed us to play at making little sandbox molds, scooping the sand, and incorporating the Chelsea doll into play. That set had previously come with the teeny tiny little container of a kinetic sand like material, but having an ample amount was really fun.

However, we discovered the problem with this stuff about 1/2 hour after cleaning up. I walked past the hard floor area where we had cleaned up afterwards, and nearly fell on my butt. I had already, I thought, cleaned up all the pieces of clay on the floor and given one or two areas a quick wipe down with cleaner, so I was puzzled as to why the floor was so slippery. I cleaned the floor there, and walked around and forgot about it for about five more minutes, when I walked by and almost fell on my butt in another spot. Then my husband almost fell. Then my child did fall. I cleaned the floor thoroughly and there were still patches of occasional area that were just ridiculously slippery, and I don't really understand how it withstood numerous attacks with normal household cleaners. But for days we were discovering slippery areas on our floor that made it really not safe.

So I would give the caveat that if you are going to allow your children to play with kinetic sand, do so outside so that you do not end up with a dangerous situation on your own hard floors.
text_fidelity_b: Kinetic Sand, Bake Shoppe Playset with 1lb of Kinetic Sand and 16 Tools and Molds, for Ages 3 and up

Using this kit, it's possible to make 8 different remote control construction vehicles (forklifts, bulldozers, etc,), or experiment and create your own thing. What I think is most impressive is that this kit can be used with children as young as 6 years old, if you believe the ages on the box.

Like all of the times that I've tried to build from the instructions, Daddy had to do most of the work when my daughter lost interest, although she's on the lower end of the recommended spectrum. The kit is easy, but it's not a cakewalk, and I don't think she could have done it on her own, but she did help, and was pleased to play with the result. The remote control aspect really sets this well above most building toys, and now she's asking me to build new stuff for her all the time.

4 cubes butter, softened
2 heaping cups dark brown sugar (packed, then heap that shiz)
½ cups white sugar
2 tablespoons vanilla
1 ½ teaspoon salt
1 ½ teaspoons baking soda
3 eggs
6 cups flour
1 bag chocolate chips (semi-sweet or sweet)

Mix BY HAND all ingredients, except flour and chips (mixing by hand makes them taste better, trust me).
Then add flour and chips and stir BY HAND. Bake @ 350 for 9-11 minutes on ungreased cookie sheet. Enjoy the preciouses.
Note: makes a buttload of cookies, so you might want to halve the recipe.

Minnie Mouse's Home Sweet Headquarters is a 4-level dollhouse playset with five rooms of play and features three figures, 12 play pieces, an elevator, and Minnie's magic Turnstyler fashion closet. This little Minne Mouse playhouse is just adorable! Perfect for toddlers and preschool children. It is a replica of Minnie's house from the Disney Channel, Disney Junior show called, "Happy Helpers Adventures." The playhouse is called, "Minnie Mouse's Home Sweet Headquarters," and in the show it is located in the town of Hot Dog Hills. This house is not just Minnie's home on the show, but it is also the business headquarters for Minnie and Daisy Duck's business, "Happy Helpers." The house has five rooms and four levels. There is a cute elevator leading to the second floor, and a "Turnstyler" closet which contains three different Happy Helpers outfits (note they are pictures of clothing rather than actual clothing that a child could put on Minnie).

Minnie's Home Sweet Headquarters set includes three 3-inch poseable figures, Minnie, Daisy, and Figaro (the kitty from the film, Pinnochio), as well as 12 accessory play pieces, including two beds, a vanity, and two desks just like the ones on the Disney show. There are also a spa tub, a hairdryer, and an oven and serving cart in the kitchen, and Figaro has his own pet food and bowl.

This play house requires a small bit of assembly, but even I managed it easily, and I am definitely not good at putting things together.

I really appreciate that this is not a typical empty doll house. It's great that it comes with furniture and other interesting pieces and the three occupants, who are the main characters from a child-favorite Disney TV show, Daisy Duck, Figaro and, of course, Minnie Mouse. There are lots of lovely, bright colors throughout the house, with Minnie's signature color of pink predominating. I especially am impressed with the little elevator that goes up and down, the rotating closet and the fact that the house's doors open and close.

This has turned out to be a very popular gift with my 20-month-old granddaughter. She loves it now, and she can continue to enjoy for several more years to come.

A terrific Christmas present!
text_fidelity_b: Minnie Mouse's Home Sweet Headquarters is a 4-level dollhouse playset with five rooms of play and features three figures, 12 play pieces, an elevator, and Minnie's magic Turnstyler fashion closet.

text_fidelity_a:
Thames and Kosmos Remote-Control Machines DLX It came with a defective remote. Emailing the committee company did nothing, but when I called they shipped me out a new one right away. There is an led on top of the remote. If it doesn't light, you have a bad remote.

The manual starts with a system test and then goes through the projects. The projects are rated in difficulty one through three and the first one on the book is a level the robotic arm that does not balance well as designed. It can be fixed easily, and figuring out how is very educational. If it is too difficult, I suggest start with a level one project. Of course, once you get it running, you've got a new RC toy to play with, and this kit can make at least 20 of them. More if your child designs her own.

The directions are just clear enough to build all of the projects, but they don't entirely spoon feed you. This toy demands your child think and reason; following instructions blindly won't be good enough. The higher the difficulty, the more the builder is required to reason on her own.

Robotics is the next big technical revolution, and this is a brilliant, affordable introduction to the field. I would say this class of toy is as important for today's kids as the Commodore 64 was for budding computer programs back is the 1980s, and this particular kit is a brilliant example of the type. It also happens to be fun for kids and adults, so much so the kids won't realize they're learning.

You will need a lot of batteries for this, five AA to be exact, and they are not included. Rechargeables will make this so much easier.
text_fidelity_b: Thames and Kosmos Remote-Control Machines DLX

text_fidelity_a:
Hot Wheels Track Builder Build Your Race Playset There's a lot to love about sets like this that can be combined with other sets and used in creative ways. However, I'll say right up front that the whole point of getting this one is that you get the power booster, and the power booster, in my view, could use a big overhaul in the design.

Is it fun? Yes, without a doubt, the power booster is pretty fun. The problem? First of all, it takes 4 D batteries. Who uses D batteries nowadays? I'm lucky that we had just the right number of D battery adapters that allow us to use AA batteries instead, because otherwise I would have been in for a trip to the grocery store and I don't think it would've come cheap. What a power hog!

Second, the battery area needs to be taken apart with a screwdriver. This is fine for toys meant for the under three crowd, but for kids old enough to use a hot wheels set, it seems a little excessive and pretty irritating that every time a new set of batteries I need to become Mr. fix it and get out a screwdriver.

Third, when you actually go to play with it, the power booster is either on or off. So when the kid forgets about the hot wheels set and wanders off to go do something else, it's still sitting there using up your expensive D cell batteries. It's also noisy. I would've much preferred a button on the top that is easy for children to press that makes it work for a short period of time, such as 30 seconds. I'm guessing it is too much to ask to have a motion sensor turn it on or off or anything like that, so a limited time button that the child can find easily and press in the midst of gameplay without turning the power booster upside down would have been ideal.

That said, I think my primary criteria for evaluating hot wheels set is whether it is fun. Not fun for me, but fun for my kids. With only a little bit of help getting things set up, my three-year-old has been playing with this vigorously for two days and shows no signs of getting bored with it. We actually have a manual hot wheels ejecter to where you pull the lever back and press a button to make the car go really fast, and instead of using the power booster, we set that up for him to play with it on his own. The power booster is fun for when you make a big elaborate set up and are playing with a group of kids or with a parent for an extended period of time but to be honest I think when the batteries run down we may not replace them until there is a compelling reason to do so. It's just too noisy, and requires too much intervention from the parent to turn it on and off when it is needed and not just leave it noisily running and eating up our batteries.

The loop the loop works great with either the power booster or the manual ejection thing we already owned, and the tracks of course work with all of our other hot wheels sets.

I would probably recommend this most for people who have multiple children who will be playing with large and extended sets of hot wheels for 30 minutes or longer at a stretch. Otherwise, the power booster seems silly and kind of a waste.
text_fidelity_b: Hot Wheels Track Builder Build Your Race Playset

Dimension - A 3D Fast-Paced Puzzle Game from Kosmos | Up to 4 Players, for Fans of Strategy, Quick-Thinking & Logic | Parents' Choice Silver Honor & Oppenheim Toy Portfolio Platinum Award Winner Though it can at times feel a bit simple, overall Dimension is a fun game that plays quickly and makes for fast, easy to learn family fun.

Packaging and materials: everything in its place, easily held in place, all in good shape, no excessive packaging, easy to open and easy to store back in the box. The balls have a good sense of heft to them, stack easily in their spots, and are well-made. Our son dropped a good number of them the first few times playing and after the first few, our nervousness about the balls breaking or chipping disappeared (though we still wished he’d control their rolls a bit better . . . ) Cards are also well-made, as our the playing boards--heavy stock that come with stick-on feet to hold them slightly off the table surface so the balls don’t move around too easily. All in all, construction is a plus.

Directions: For the most part, directions are quite clear and are pretty minimal. The directions also offer up a few variant forms of the game for making things easier or more challenging, though to be honest, anyone could have come up with those pretty easily and quickly (for instance, upping the number of challenges one has to meet)

Game play.
You each take some point markers to start, and place your 15 spheres--five trios of different colors-- in your game board (again, the balls rest solidly in their holes).

The center of the game board is where you will build patterns with the balls depending on the card challenges. There are seven spaces in the building area, and you can build upward from those spaces, employing up to three layers and up to 11 spheres (7 in your bottom layer, three in the middle layer, and one on top).

You lay out six cards, each one detailing a particular challenge you must meet when you build your patterns. Some examples:
Two specific colors must touch (i.e. somewhere in your pattern, a blue sphere must contact a white sphere
Two specific colors must not touch
You must use a specific number of a particular color
One color must outnumber another (i.e. you must have more green spheres than white spheres)
Two colors must total a specific number (i.e. between blue and white spheres, you must total 4: 1 blue and 3 white, 2 and 2, 1 white and 3 blue)
A particular color cannot be laid atop any of the other colors
A particular color cannot have any of the other colors put on top of it (i.e. your green spheres must be the topmost layer)

once the cards are laid out, you turn over a one-minute timer and try and create a 3-dimensional pattern/pyramid that will meet as many of the challenges as possible.

You get one point for each challenge you meet and lose two points for each one you miss. There is a bonus for meeting all six and/or using all the colors. You also get more points the more spheres you use, though you’ll have to weigh quickly whether adding more spheres to get more points might break a rule and thus lose more than you gain (for instance, adding another blue sphere would get you a point, but if in doing so you broke a rule by having it touch a green sphere, you would lose two points).

As you can see, sometimes the rules may conflict (you might, for instance, get a card that says blue and white must touch and another that says blue and white cannot touch). In those cases, each player decides for him/herself which challenge they choose to ignore.

An entire game is six rounds and most points wins.

It goes very quickly and as you might guess, the speed and difficulty of each round is determined by the combination of cards. Sometimes all three of us were done well before the timer, other times we were all caught with spheres still in our hands trying to figure out where to add or remove a color. And sometimes you’d smoothly and confidently total up your six points for meeting all the challenges and other times as you were oh so cockily adding another challenge to your list you’d suddenly realize, “Doh--how did I end up with a green touching a blue?!”

Mostly the game moves along quickly and the combinations are decently challenging, though we all thought we’d probably move on to doing 8 challenges soon to up the difficulty even more. The only other point I’d make is an electronic timer would be nice as you’re all concentrating so hard on your pyramid that we’d often miss the time running out, or you’d just pluck off a ball to replace with another when someone noticed it was done and you were stuck. We’ve therefore actually taken to using one of our iPhones as a timer to give us a 10-second beep before the full time runs out.

The other nice thing about the game is it is pretty easily modified for playing to younger levels--dump the timer, drop a color, uses only three or four cards. The game can grow with your kids. Certainly even 5-8 year olds can play simpler versions and then grow into more difficult challenges. Fun to play, a bit different, uses some different skills. Recommended.
text_fidelity_b: Dimension - A 3D Fast-Paced Puzzle Game from Kosmos | Up to 4 Players, for Fans of Strategy, Quick-Thinking & Logic | Parents' Choice Silver Honor & Oppenheim Toy Portfolio Platinum Award Winner

Insect Lore - Butterfly Growing Kit - Butterfly Habitat Kit with Voucher to Redeem 5 Caterpillars, STEM Journal, Butterfly Feeder & More – Life Science & STEM Education – Butterfly Science Kit The Live Butterfly Garden by Insect Lore is a fun, hands- on educational experience that is certain to appeal to even the most stubborn, disinterested child. With the Live Butterfly Garden, children get to observe the process of metamorphosis, right before their eyes. Starting with caterpillars, children watch the little critters eat food, create a cocoon, and then transform into fully grown adult butterflies. The butterflies can then be observed in their habitat for a while before setting free.

This butterfly garden is great for dozens of reasons, the most obvious of which is the educational value. Reading about insects and metamorphosis is one thing, but seeing the process live is another thing entirely. Kids get to learn how caterpillars/butterflies live, eat, and thrive; how to care for them; etc. They get to observe the caterpillars and butterflies at play and watch the butterflies eat their food, which is provided in the package. The caterpillars that come with the Live Butterfly Garden are painted ladies, which are not very common and will not be recognized by most children. However, most kids won't care- the fun of watching these small caterpillars transform into butterflies will have many kids gazing in awe, and prompt them to ask many questions.

This educational toy is a huge hit and my kids loved it, but there were a few small issues. One was waiting for the caterpillars to arrive in the mail. To get the caterpillars, you have to mail in an included certificate, along with a check, and then wait. It seems like an eternity, especially from the perspective of young children, and it took longer than expected. Anther problem was parting with the butterflies. Once you have the caterpillars and they have transformed into adult butterflies, the next problem will be setting them free. Kids will grow attached to their small, winged friends and will not want to let them go. Another minor issue is with the transferring of the caterpillars from their small container- the one you receive in the mail- into the actual habitat. The container that the caterpillars arrive in has a paper area at the top, where the caterpillars will hang as they spin their cocoons. This paper section is fairly easy to remove, but the problem is that the cocoons are very delicately attached, and that means that some will fall off when the transfer is made. You will need to pin this piece of paper to the inside of the butterfly garden, but the kit doesn't include any pins. Safety pins or straight pins work, and it would have been nice if these were included in the kit.

Still, when all factors are considered, the Live Butterfly Garden is worth the purchase and young children will enjoy the educational experience. Sure, it could be improved a little bit by making a few minor changes, but this is still a very good toy and considering my kid's fascination with the process, along with the educational value, it earns an easy recommendation.
text_fidelity_b: Insect Lore - Butterfly Growing Kit - Butterfly Habitat Kit with Voucher to Redeem 5 Caterpillars, STEM Journal, Butterfly Feeder & More – Life Science & STEM Education – Butterfly Science Kit

Crayola Super Tips Washable Markers Age 3+ - 50 Count I'll admit it: I'm an adult who loves to color. I find it a great way to relax, and there are some amazing "coloring books for adults" gaining popularity these days (Johanna Basford, Angie Grace, etc.). And there are whole communities of "colorists" popping up on social media.

So naturally, I'm looking for different mediums to use when I color. I've used colored pencils and gel pens, so I figured it was time to branch out into the marker arena. Someone suggested starting with these as they're water-based rather than alcohol-based, and Amazon has them at a good price, so I got the 50-ct set.

Overall, I'm pleased. There is a good selection of colors, several shades of each, which helps to bring some variety into th mix.

What I DON'T like (and this seems to be a problem for ALL coloring mediums): the actual color of the pen/pencil/etc. almost NEVER matches the color of the cap/barrel/etc. I realize that colors will look different depending on the type a "color" of paper used as the background, but seriously, some of these are WAY off. I find myself having to make a "cheat sheet" on the paper I'm using just so I can get a clear picture of how the various colors REALLY look.

Like I said, this isn't just a problem with Crayola, but they make it a little more difficult because the pens have NO distinguishing markings on them whatsoever to designate a color number or code. I ended up putting little pieces of masking tape on each pen and numbering them myself just so I can keep the color charts coordinated.

All that aside, they work great once you figure out the colors. Colors are vibrant, and I had very little "bleed through" or feathering in an Angie Grace book. Bleed through and feathering depend a great deal on the paper used, so bear that in mind and ALWAYS test before coloring.

Overall​, I like these - don't "love" them, but they're good quality water-based markers at a very good price.
text_fidelity_b: Crayola Super Tips Washable Markers Age 3+ - 50 Count

text_fidelity_a:
Civilization A New Dawn Board Game | Tactical Strategy Game for Adults and Teens Based on the Hit Video Game Series | Ages 14+ | 2-4 Players | Average Playtime 1-2 Hours | Made by Fantasy Flight Games Short version of the review: it’s a fun game with a pretty good first-game learning curve that settles in pretty quickly in subsequent games. It can be long (though you can adjust it). We’ll add it to our rotation of “lengthy” games

Longer version

1) Packing
I’m going to ding the game for packaging because while everything comes fine (as is typical, there’s a lot of popping pieces out of their cardboard sheets), I like when games include easy ways of keeping thing together and/or organized once you’ve played the first game. Even if it’s as minimal as separate small plastic bags. We used our own tiny bags (we’ve learned to keep ones that do come with other games if they’re extra thanks to consolidation) and a few regular small baggies, but I don’t think it’s too much to ask that those things be included

2) Materials
All the materials seem of good quality. Cards are not super-thick but they’re not at all flimsy, the non-plastic pieces feel solid and you don’t have any sense that they’ll start coming apart or getting dented/torn. The plastic cities are a nice touch, but the capital cities could perhaps have been made a little more distinctive. Not at all a big deal; a close look is all you need.

3) Instructions
The big sheet of instructions is fine. Generally clear and well written, with a few “clarification” points at the end, which is a nice touch. We had a few questions that weren’t included, but they were easy to find online. A few individual player cards with a stripped down bit of instruction for quick, easy reference would have been nice to toss in

4) Set up
As noted (and as is usual for these types of games) there’s a lot of popping things out and organizing. Once that’s done the first time, set-up is relatively quick. You put together some map tiles which is easy enough (though this 50+-year-old wouldn’t have minded if the organizing numbers were a little bigger on each tile). Each player gets tokens, a set of cards five of which are laid out in a particular order under their “Focus” bar (the cards are in these areas: Military, Technology, Culture, Economy, Industry), a set of “diplomacy” cards, a “leader” card (who they “play”—Cleopatra for instance), a few caravans (little wagons used for trading). After you’ve done it a few times it’s a pretty quick set-up. You also set up some cards to the side of the play area (World Wonder cards and City-State Diplomacy Cards and Victory Cards (these are what determine how the game is won). This is always an issue in these sorts of game because of course they’re not going to be truly “visible” to all the players. Someone is going to have to move or ask to see them to see what they say (some change throughout the game). I have no idea how to get around that though; it’s just a matter of physical setting.

5) game play
I’m not going to detail it. But generally, the Victory cards have two “agendas” on them, such as build two Wonders of the World, and a player who achieves one agenda from each of the cards is the winner (this is nice because you can shorten the game if desired by simply playing with fewer Victory cards). As far as the play itself
1) Players can “resolve” (do what it says) any one of the five cards below their Focus bar. This might mean building a city, attacking someone, moving a caravan, laying out a “Control” piece to claim a hex space (i.e. territory).
2) Once they’ve done that, that card gets move to slot one under the bar and all the others move one slot to the right. This is key because the slot number affects how the card is resolved. For instance, when you attack using your military card, you roll a die and add the slot number (and possibly other bonuses) to your roll. So you’re going to want to attack when that card is in the 4 or 5 position typically, not the 1 or 2 slot. This adds a nice bit of complexity to your action choices.

That’s pretty much the gameplay for players. A few other factor include
1) You can swap out a card under your focus by advancing your “Tech” counter a certain number (you do that using one of the cards). Once you hit a certain level, you can exchange one low level card for one that’s a bit more powerful. There are 4 levels of cards.
2) Barbarian tokens on the board move at regular periods and they can end up destroying one of your caravans or claiming territory from you (which affects how much money your cities earn and how much you can advance)
3) Caravans allow you to gain trade tokens that can be used to increase the impact of your cards. For example, if you have two trade tokens on your military card, you can spend one or both to add a bonus to your roll. Caravans can also garner you another player’s Diplomacy card, which has certain benefits dependent on the card.
4) Placing a control tokens mean you’ve claimed territory (that particular space), which is necessary for collecting trade tokens (a “mature” city garners you a set number of trade tokens once you’ve “controlled” all adjacent tiles), collecting resources such as marble or diamonds, or for building cities (your build cities a certain number of spaces from a space you’ve controlled with a token).
5) The terrain has an impact on your choices. In order of scaled “easiness”, the terrains are 1-grasslands, 2-hills, 3-forest, 4-desert, and 5-mountains. To travel through a desert is considered difficult, so that 4 means your Economy card (the one that moves your caravan) needs to be in the 4 or 5 slot. Similary, to build a city in a mountain space means your Industry card has to be in the 5 slot.

There are more rules and factors that come into play, but that’s the general gist. As noted at the start, I’d say the learning curve is relatively steep the first time ( a lot of going back to the instruction booklet), but past the first game or two, it comes pretty easily. I’ve certainly played games with a far steeper curve and one that takes longer to get to know game play well. If I were ranking learning curves on a ten-point scale, I’d probably put this around a 6.

Turns move slowly the first time or two as people try to remember what they can do, what they need to do, etc. But after the first hour each player moves pretty quickly through their turns as you’ve gotten used to how to deal with the complexities of those shifting slots under the Focus bar. As people get closer to each other, things slow again as players try and figure out cost-benefit of attacking, but then as before, after a few attacks those move quickly.

I liked the game quite a bit. More than my two family members, but I tend to have more patience for the slowness of things and I mind long game less than they do. They did like it enough to play again. And as mentioned, I like that you can self-adjust your length simply by cutting out one of the agendas. It’s a game we’ll definitely keep and keep playing.
text_fidelity_b: Civilization A New Dawn Board Game | Tactical Strategy Game for Adults and Teens Based on the Hit Video Game Series | Ages 14+ | 2-4 Players | Average Playtime 1-2 Hours | Made by Fantasy Flight Games

text_fidelity_a:
Schleich Dinosaurs, Realistic Large Dinosaur Toys for Boys and Girls, Barapasaurus Toy Figurine, Ages 4+ We absolutely love our dinosaurs, dragons, and lifelike statues of real animals from this brand, and this extra-large dinosaur is no exception. The thing you should know about these is that they are a very hard resin like material. This makes them much better for children who are old enough to use the statues responsibly and not bash them on things such as their little sister, because they are very hard and heavy and have absolutely no give to them. On this particular model, the end of the tail is the most dangerous part aside from the sheer size and weight of the overall piece.

This dinosaur is much larger than the cheapo dinosaurs that you get in multi-packs that are made in China, and the level of craftsmanship and detail here is sufficient for even the most exacting dinosaur connoisseur. That said, though the description talks about scoop shaped teeth being a major part of what makes this dinosaur cool, I was unable to really discern much scoop detail on the teeth, given the relative size of the teeth versus the relative size of the dinosaur. Just something to be aware of. But that's not me complaining about the level of detail.

I love the artistic detailing on the hide, the bluish bumps on the back, the little spines, and the huge amount of expression in the face. My toddler son is just beginning a dinosaur phase and enjoyed stomping this large dinosaur through his truck collection and roaring with great feeling. I think that as his knowledge of dinosaurs expands, so will his appreciation of all the small differentiating details that give this dinosaur personality, character, and most importantly, accuracy.

As long as you are aware of the hard and heavy resin material used to create these, you will be deeply impressed by the detailing, durability, and potential for imaginative play inherent in the figure.
text_fidelity_b: Schleich Dinosaurs, Realistic Large Dinosaur Toys for Boys and Girls, Barapasaurus Toy Figurine, Ages 4+

text_fidelity_a:
Barbie Rainbow Hair Doll I have been around Barbie dolls my entire life. My mom collected them and my sister got into it. My daughter has had a few here and there, but none of them was the quality that this doll is. I did not expect it to be fantastic quality, but it even fell short of my lower expectations.

WHAT IS THE DOLL LIKE?
The doll comes in a clear plastic package which is not overly attractive, in fact it looks stark and not like the usual Barbie stuff. The doll itself is packaged with two pieces of plastic sticking out from inside her head. It is then attached to the board in the back so you have to cut those pieces to get it off of the backing. That means you have to be careful of the hair. Once you managed to do this, you have to stick the plastic ends back into the skull of the doll to keep the sharp ends from pricking your child or you.

The outfit is kind of cute and the colors are attractive. The doll itself is a rigid plastic doll- not the bendable twist and turn type that they have had in the past. The head piece has a knob type attachment which makes it able to move in almost any direction. The problem is in this case, the head is so easy to move it is borderline bobble head.

HOW DOES THE HAIR COLOR WORK?
The hair color looked like it would be a lot of fun! It has a plastic piece that is similar to a flat iron in shape. Inside the *flat iron* piece are a group of colored waxy blocks. The idea is that you comb the doll's hair and separate it into strands. You press the flat iron type piece over the hair, squeeze it shut as you draw the hair through and it leaves the color on the hair.

The hair is waxy in feel, probably to make the color work better than traditional Barbie hair. In this case, however, it does not seem to do much for the process. The hair colors are not too great. They come off as crumbly and waxy and very spotty on the hair. If you run your fingers over it, you will get some on your fingers. This will stain so if your child plays with this near anything white or light colored, it could stain it.

The color blocks are almost like you mix waxy crayons with silicone to make it a bit softer. The result is uneven kind of unimpressive color on the hair. It is not overly bright and does not look like the pictures promised.

THE BOTTOM LINE
My daughter was not impressed by this doll. The body is very rigid, making for a boring play toy. The hair is very uneven and has a waxy feel to it. The colors come out crumbly and uneven, and color blocks probably will only last for a day or two of constant play and then run out. The colors will stain some things so if you plan to let your child run free with this, you may regret it if you have anything white you don't want stained. The head is so easily moved that it is unpleasant to play with and use. The outfit is cute and colorful and the shoes are not too bad either.

My daughter kept saying that she expected more substantial color that was like a watercolor marker or something instead of a crumbly waxy substance that barely sticks to the hair in a few random spots. She kept taking out her other Barbie dolls and saying how much more she liked those. I give this two stars because it has a nice outfit, and if you want a disposable toy for your child, it will serve the purpose. If you want a sturdy toy they will play with over and over, I am thinking this might not be it for you.
text_fidelity_b: Barbie Rainbow Hair Doll

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Star Wars: A New Hope Imperial Star Destroyer 75252 Building Kit (4,784 Pieces) The first thing I noticed about this set was the weight. This is the first LEGO set that I've gotten that I would actually describe as heavy. That's a lot of brick. The box is nice, and contains several smaller boxes. Those boxes have some blueprint art on them, but no useful labeling as to where to begin. You need to open them all anyway, because the unlabeled bags of large parts are mixed in with some of the later bags, despite being needed early on. The bag numbering only goes up to about 20, but there are many bags for each number and the bags have bags in them. The instruction book is huge and spiral bound, with some nice history in the early pages.

The set goes together surprisingly quickly early on, starting with the display base and docking clamps, which the ship is built on, with sections being build and then clipped on. The internal support structure is well engineered and solid. You get a good impression of the overall size and shape of the ship by the time you are done with bag 2.

At first glance, this may look like a tedious grey set where all the parts look the same, but the insides are brightly colored. This is really nice because the parts being built are often rotated between panels, and the colors really help with both finding the parts and orienting with the instructions. When you're done, it also makes it easy to spot anything you missed, because the grey exterior will have rainbow colors there.

One disappointment is the thin area down the sides of the ship. I like them fine individually, but the instructions have you build them identically, so rather than being bilaterally symmetrical, one side looks like it's upside down compared to the other. I understand this saved them some pages, and made construction a little easier, but I would've appreciated a heads up so I could build it mirrored, since I think that would've worked out fine, at least for the greebles on the outside. I may actually take one side apart and redo it, though It's the kind of detail that an observer might not notice because this thing is so big. There are other areas that are more obviously asymmetrical, which is true to the movie, but looks really jarring to me the way they implemented it.

After completing it, I feel like it was designed by two different teams of people. The interior structure is an awesome feat of engineering, and so sturdy you can carry the whole thing by an interior handle, despite its great weight, and they did it with all existing parts. The exterior is about as expected in a Lego set. The transition between the two is weak. Brushing against it risks knocking things off. Sometimes it's just some barely attached pieces on the back, other times something obviously comes apart inside that's going to take some doing to get to and fix. The different sections are often just resting loosely on each other and sometimes look uneven. There is a tiny and comically inadequate clip to hold the four sections of the front in alignment. You may want to think about what you're going to do with it when it's done. It's large, heavy, and oddly shaped. Comes on a nice stand though.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Star Wars: A New Hope Imperial Star Destroyer 75252 Building Kit (4,784 Pieces)

VTech Go! Go! Smart Wheels Race & Play Adventure Park 5 stars for the toy itself. 0 stars for the directions - they are awful! The pictures are in blurry black and white, and the wording is confusing. It took me far too long to put together, but I was impressed by the finished product.

First of all - this is big! Look carefully at the specs on this toy to see if it will fit well (or dominate) your play space. The colors and designs are bright and cheerful, which I like. There are a few specific mechanical steps to make this work right with the car, and I worried that it would be too complicated for my 2yo granddaughter. (1) The arm needs to be clicked down into position, (2) you need to wind the car up the ramp (and the crank for that is tricky - if you let go just a little, it slides back to the bottom), then once the car slides down the ramp into the cradle you need to (3) release the arm for the catapult to launch down the second slide. Again - sounds complicated, right? But my granddaughter mastered it in no time! I was surprised and happy about that.

I was also very happy that she played with this over and over. She never seemed to get bored with it. The little car plays music and phrases as it goes along, and even when all the steps didn't go perfectly (ie: the car crashed), my granddaughter was amused. One quick note: some of the joints seem to come apart easily, and since toddlers are a little rough, we needed to keep an eye on this. Still, this will be a great toy that grows with our grandkids!
text_fidelity_b: VTech Go! Go! Smart Wheels Race & Play Adventure Park

Kelsyus Premium Floating Lounger XL with Fast Inflation, Inflatable Recliner Chair, Lake & Pool Float for Adults with Cup Holder, Amazon Exclusive I bought this item and, for the most part, enjoyed its design, but...
1. It's just about impossible to inflate or deflate because of the valves; standard foot pumps do not work with these valves and doing it by mouth (which is what I ended up doing) is extremely tedious, because there is not enough length to hold it in your mouth to pinch it for opening the valve. Deflating the main air chamber is likewise nearly impossible, this time because that chamber is composed of both the main ring and the air pillow -- it would have been a lot smarter to use three chambers. (The second, tiny air chamber to float the footholder, does not hold much air and so is not as much of a problem.)
2. the netting that serves as seat is very flimsy, yet too closed and acts a magnet collecting every floating insect; cleaning that is not as simple as it seems, because the fully inflated, wet lounger is something of a handful and the netting does not want to let go.
The position in which one floats, however, is excellent -- I just wish the manufacturer (or another manufacturer) would make a version that is easy to inflate and deflate and does not trap everything that floats.

Just My Style Name Bracelet Maker by Horizon Group USA I think this kit is just "ok". My 6yo was far more impressed than I was.
My main problem with this kit is that there is no way anyone could string these beads. All thread included is far to thick for the tiny bead holes. My daughter was excited to use a real needle for the first time though. Pictured next to the needed is a needle threader (threaders can be picked up for $1 at your local box if they still have a sewing dept).
The string she used to make her bead bracelet was silky smooth. It made the beading process easier... but the bracelet broke three minutes after she finished. I triple knotting it off too and that wasn't strong enough to keep the knot together. I'd recommend dotting the knot with a drop of glue or clear nail polish to make it hold.
In addition, I think this kit is divided in half; made for two different age groups. Younger children who would be interested in beading part probably won't be ready for friendship braclet weaving for a few more years. And just the same, I think older girls might find the beading process too juvenile. So if your looking for a friendship bracelet kit, I don't see a lot of value in this kit.
These is also a lot of excess packaging to make what you get seem bigger than it is. I feel like this is something that I would have pick up at five below, so $13 feels overpriced to me.
(My daughter wanted to use her own round letter beads; but she could have used the square letter beads that came in this kit just the same)
text_fidelity_b: Just My Style Name Bracelet Maker by Horizon Group USA
